sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Engineer David Mummery designed the Swimmer Turbine, a 50kW tidal generator made from fiberglass and steel. Developed by Flex Marine Power, the device was assembled and launched down a slipway by local fishermen on Islay after earlier testing in Northern Ireland and elsewhere in Scotland.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Unlike utility-scale tidal projects, the ultra-compact turbine can be shipped in a container and built locally without heavy cranes. Anchored invisibly to the seabed, it produces enough electricity for about 30 homes, offering coastal communities direct control over local renewable energy.

gist: The Orionid meteor shower is active until 7 November, peaking overnight on 21-22 October.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The Orionid meteor shower has become active as Earth travels through a trail of dust and debris shed by Halley's Comet. Tiny particles enter the atmosphere at around 41 miles per second, creating glowing trails that can briefly linger in the night sky.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The shower peaks overnight from 21 to 22 October, offering up to 20 meteors per hour in dark areas. Rain across the UK is expected to move away early during the peak night, but wetter and windier weather may follow later in the week. Activity continues until 7 November, though light from the approaching full Moon on 26 October may obscure fainter meteors.

sections.text: At annual meetings in Bangkok, the World Bank urged developing nations to create specialised small AI models. Chief knowledge officer Paschal Donohoe stated these models operate on mobile phones with low connectivity and in local languages, helping meet specific needs such as agricultural soil analysis in India. Meanwhile, IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva called on governments to provide essential preconditions, including electricity, digital infrastructure and safety from bad actors.

sections.text: Donohoe said economic development that once required centuries could now occur within decades if technology matches local requirements. However, substantial barriers remain; a World Bank report noted that nearly a third of rural schools in sub-Saharan Africa lack electricity and over two-thirds lack reliable internet. Georgieva also warned that 40% of global jobs could be augmented or eliminated, severely affecting young workers entering the labour market.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Green Party members voted 1,022 to 813 to approve a motion equating Zionism with racism. Leader Zack Polanski did not vote on the motion but told the BBC he will not overturn it, respecting the democratic will of members. He described Zionism in practical application as racist, argued no state has a right to exist under international law, and denied the motion was controversial, though media outlets noted it caused major fallout.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The vote sparked backlash from MPs, Jewish campaigners, the government and European Greens. It divided the party, drew criticism from figures including Jewish Greens head Vivien Lichtenstein, and overshadowed Polanski's by-election campaign in Holborn and St Pancras, where he finished second. Green MP Ellie Chowns and others have urged a review of party decision-making rules due to low turnout.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The motion remains party policy for two years until 2028. Polanski aims to amend it at the first available opportunity to support Israelis and Palestinians determining their own future.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Margaret Hamilton, the computer scientist who developed the flight software for Nasa's Apollo missions, has died aged 90. She headed the software team at the MIT Instrumentation Laboratory, creating the guidance systems that navigated spacecraft to the lunar surface.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Hamilton coined the phrase "software engineering" and established rigorous simulation procedures that prevented software failures across crewed Apollo flights. During Apollo 11, her guidance allowed flight controllers to bypass landing alarms caused by a radar switch. Furthermore, her team pioneered the use of silicon-integrated circuits, laying groundwork for modern electronics and encouraging generations of women to enter technical disciplines.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Modern romantasy novels follow a tradition of medieval fairy romance that began in French courts during the late 1100s. These popular tales featured adventurous plots, crystal palaces, and sexually active fairies. They circulated widely across Europe before falling out of fashion in the late 1500s as depictions of fairies changed.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Both medieval romance and modern romantasy offered safe spaces for women to explore desires free from societal expectations of chastity. The stories frequently inverted conventional gender roles, featuring powerful fairy queens who rescued distressed knights. Despite shaping enduring literature, both historical and contemporary works have faced dismissal and ridicule from critics primarily because women produce and consume them.

articles.title: The problem with telling people the world is ending

timeline.text: The problem with telling people the world is ending

gist: Negative headlines increase online clicks but doom-laden messaging discourages real-world action.
Feelings of dread and helplessness can paralyse the public during serious global crises.
Promoting scientific consensus and hope mobilises people far more effectively than fear.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Researchers evaluated 22,743 headline experiments from Upworthy.com and tested eleven climate messages on 59,440 participants across 63 countries. The analysis showed that while negative wording attracted clicks and doomsday messages were widely shared on social media, frightening texts proved the least effective at encouraging practical efforts to mitigate climate change.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Constant exposure to apocalyptic warnings engenders helplessness rather than motivating change. Inaction becomes a default response when people feel problems are insurmountable. Conversely, sober presentations of scientific consensus and messages emphasising the emotional rewards of action, such as hope and connection, significantly boost real engagement and support for solutions.

fivew: Research examined how negative messaging and doom-laden narratives influence public engagement and action.
The climate messaging study included participants across 63 countries.
To determine which forms of crisis communication effectively mobilise people to take real action.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A kerosene spill spread almost 2.5 miles along the River Taff, affecting areas such as Nantgarw and Taffs Well. Natural Resources Wales located the source on Friday evening and deployed absorbent materials alongside South Wales Fire and Rescue Service to limit fuel entering the water. Residents reported overpowering fumes and dead fish.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: People were told to close windows and doors as fumes caused eye irritation. One resident reported that up to 25,000 litres had entered the river, while a former fire service protection officer warned that recovery would take years because kerosene does not mix with water.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Officers continue investigating how the fuel reached the drainage system, aiming to stop the pollution completely and collect evidence. Natural Resources Wales is also analysing samples to establish the spill's environmental impact.

gist: Tony Hall has lived in the UK for 50 years after arriving from Barbados.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Tony Hall arrived in the UK from Barbados in 1976 at age 12. In 2001, he was convicted of conspiracy to rob and having a firearm with intent, serving eight years in prison. sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The case highlights ongoing issues from the Windrush scandal, where people with long-term UK ties face deportation and administrative limbo. Critics point to the unfairness of prolonged uncertainty and double jeopardy after individuals have served their criminal sentences.

sections.heading: What happens next

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: NHS managers have warned that up to 20 smaller consultant-led maternity units across England may need to shut. While the Health Service Journal previously estimated 24 units were at risk, NHS Alliance acute lead Matthew Hopkins cited 20. The organisation stated that staffing shortages and a sharp increase in caesarean births leave smaller units unable to safely maintain round-the-clock care.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Health bosses argue consolidating services will improve safety and care quality for mothers and babies. However, closures would particularly impact rural and coastal communities, forcing women to travel much further to give birth. The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists called for alternative solutions, urging ministers to resolve pressures through workforce expansion and training rather than closures.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: A government taskforce on maternity and neonatal care will release recommendations before Christmas, which will form a national action plan announced by Health Secretary Yvette Cooper. Meanwhile, in Devon, services at Barnstaple remain suspended ahead of an October readiness assessment.

gist: Alberta voters are deciding whether to pursue a binding referendum on leaving Canada.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Albertans went to the polls to vote on whether to begin the legal process for a binding independence referendum. Premier Danielle Smith called the vote following pressure and a grassroots petition, though she opposes separation. Voters also faced nine additional referendum questions covering matters such as immigration, social programmes and judicial appointments.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Separatists argue Ottawa's environmental policies constrain Alberta's fossil fuel wealth. Conversely, opponents, including Prime Minister Mark Carney, warn an exit would trigger severe financial uncertainty, lost jobs, and billions in debt. Indigenous First Nations challenged the process in court, arguing treaties prevent Alberta from having the constitutional right to separate.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Officials will count ballots by hand, with the separation question tallied first and initial results expected early Tuesday. If approved, a binding referendum could take place as early as 2027.

sections.text: The World Food Programme has cut food aid to Gaza, reducing monthly recipients from 1.6 million to 1.1 million. Daily community kitchen meals have fallen from 250,000 to 150,000, while ration boxes and cash transfers have also been reduced.

gist: Wildfires in northern boreal regions are accelerating permafrost thaw and releasing ancient carbon.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Intensifying wildfires across northern boreal forests have accelerated permafrost thaw, leading researchers and fire managers to test intervention strategies. In regions like Alaska, initiatives are trialling fire suppression and intentional burning to safeguard carbon-dense soils rather than solely defending human habitations and property.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Permafrost stores roughly twice as much carbon as the atmosphere. Intense blazes burn away the insulating organic topsoil, causing rapid thaw and releasing potent greenhouse gases. This threatens to create a feedback loop that transforms northern carbon sinks into major global emission sources.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Collaborators under the North Fire initiative plan to expand risk mapping across Alaska and Canada and test cultural burning near Fort Yukon. Meanwhile, the FireSat satellite constellation will expand into the 2030s to help detect blazes early.

gist: Threatening emails sent to 160 Northern Ireland schools are not deemed a viable threat.
Some schools shut or initiated lockdown procedures, while others opted to remain open.
Principals criticised education bodies over alleged lack of clear guidance during the incident.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: An email sent to 160 schools in Northern Ireland claimed that an explosive device had been placed inside them. Education Minister Paul Givan confirmed the threat was not considered viable. Some schools closed and sent pupils home, one entered lockdown, while others remained open following police advice.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The incident caused widespread alarm and educational disruption. School principals expressed frustration, stating they received conflicting or practically non-existent guidance from authorities, leaving them to make vital safety decisions alone. The Education Authority said it issued communications and is working closely with police.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The Police Service of Northern Ireland is conducting urgent enquiries and liaising with affected schools, with an update to be provided in due course.

timeline.text: Ferocious criticism from all sides underlines Macron’s isolation

gist: Emmanuel Macron faced fierce criticism from all political sides following violent nationwide riots and protests.
Protests over living costs and public services were hijacked by masked groups causing widespread damage.
Macron's isolation deepened amid a fiscal crisis, a deadlocked parliament, and a collapsed centrist coalition.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Violent riots and looting erupted across France during a weekend of protests involving students, teachers, trade unionists, and the gilets jaunes movement over living costs and inequality. Masked groups torched vehicles, ransacked businesses, and damaged public infrastructure. Emmanuel Macron addressed the nation, expressing anger and shame, but offered no new policy initiatives or public spending.

timeline.text: Hackers hit AI coding tool OpenCode, running up charges on users’ AI accounts

gist: Hackers breached an older system of open source AI coding agent OpenCode.
The attack affected 1.4% of users of the online platform OpenCode Console.
Attackers ran up unauthorized charges on users' connected AI accounts.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Attackers breached an older system of OpenCode overnight, affecting 1.4% of OpenCode Console users. Developers reported unauthorized charges and spending alerts on their AI accounts. While OpenCode described it as a distillation attack, skeptics called that framing an overstretch and argued it was a straightforward breach.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The incident highlighted difficulties in defending against large-scale cyberattacks when AI model safety guardrails refuse to analyse malicious payloads needed for defence work. Anthropic, Google and OpenAI blocked or worked to restore exposed keys, while refunds for unauthorised charges are underway.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: OpenCode stated that the incident remains ongoing. The company has instructed affected users to revoke and replace their API keys directly with each provider.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A researcher published an exploit chain as part of a proof-of-concept attack after submitting a bug report to Plex. sections.text: Amazon Web Services released a tool called TorchNeuron on Monday, allowing AI startups to easily move apps onto Amazon's Trainium chip by changing one line of configuration. The tool works with PyTorch and challenges Nvidia's dominant software advantage.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Nvidia's CUDA software has made its hardware the default choice for AI. TorchNeuron aims to remove this lock-in, giving developers a way to use Amazon's cloud and custom chips while potentially lowering costs.

sections.text: Presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov told the BBC that inconsistent American attack warnings had caused Ukrainian deaths. While Volodymyr Zelensky previously stated intelligence sharing resumed after a pause, Beskrestnov said missile alerts remained erratic. Beskrestnov suggested the twin measures could be deliberate American pressure to force negotiations with Russia.

sections.heading: What happens next

sections.text: Charity Kaleidoscope reported a sharp surge in ketamine detox referrals at Birchwood, rising from two cases in 2021 to 112 this year. sections.text: The substance causes swift, severe damage compared with alcohol or Class A narcotics, including memory impairment and organ failure. timeline.text: Morocco's first female prime minister caught between the king, clerics, and feminists

gist: King Mohammed VI appointed Fatima Zahra El Mansouri as Morocco's first female prime minister.
Her historic appointment has sparked debates among clerics, political figures, and feminists.
Rights activists urge her government to reform family law and improve girls' education.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: King Mohammed VI appointed Fatima Zahra El Mansouri as Morocco's first female prime minister. Her party, the Authenticity and Modernity Party, won the most seats in September's election and formed a four-party coalition holding 207 parliamentary seats.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The appointment breaks a gender barrier, but has resurfaced conservative opposition and debate over women in leadership. Rights groups hope her administration will address family law reforms and improve education access for rural girls. However, analysts note her room for manoeuvre is constrained by the monarchy and religious authorities.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: El Mansouri has not indicated whether she will push through family code reforms, leaving activists waiting to see if her government enacts actual change.

quotes.text: Her party presents itself as a modernising political force
it finally breaks a ceiling that was never broken

gist: Mayor Zohran Mamdani urged New Yorkers to challenge the rapid rollout of artificial intelligence.
Mamdani criticised federal inaction, accusing national authorities of allowing technology firms to self-regulate.
New York City has introduced school AI bans and disclosure rules for property listings.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: At an event at Webster Hall, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and activist Ilana Glazer discussed artificial intelligence. Mamdani urged New Yorkers to reject the idea that AI adoption is inevitable and argued that public officials must hold technology firms accountable.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Mamdani criticised the federal government for failing to regulate the sector, noting that national policy largely lets companies self-regulate. In response to risks, New York City has already barred AI from elementary and middle schools and mandated disclosures for AI-generated real estate listings.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Mamdani called for a different accountability framework following the current federal administration, as AI companies including Anthropic and OpenAI prepare to enter public markets.

fivew: Mayor Zohran Mamdani and activist Ilana Glazer.

timeline.text: NHS trust prosecuted over children's sepsis deaths

gist: An NHS trust faces prosecution over two children's sepsis deaths.
Court papers claim care and treatment lacked safety.
The trust will appear in court in December.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust faces three charges concerning the deaths of two young children who had sepsis. Three-year-old Zadie Ajetunmobi passed away in November 2022 after being taken to Broomfield Hospital in Essex with a high temperature and suffering a cardiac arrest. Two-year-old Selina Samarina was discharged by a doctor in April 2024 and died two days following readmission.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The Care Quality Commission is bringing the legal action under the Health and Social Care Act. Court documents allege that safe care and treatment were not delivered to the two girls.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The trust is scheduled to appear before Chelmsford Magistrates' Court in December to enter pleas regarding the charges.

fivew: Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust.

gist: Ghent’s design museum has opened a new £17m extension made largely from recycled materials.
The building features specially developed carbon-absorbing bricks made from local construction waste.
Local residents contributed to the design recommendations for the collaborative civic expansion project.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A £17m extension to the design museum in Ghent, Belgium, has been built by Carmody Groarke with local firms Atama and Re-st. The five-storey mass-timber structure connects existing museum galleries and includes public spaces shaped by recommendations from a 40-member citizens' panel.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The project uses innovative bricks made from 63% local construction waste, including discarded sinks, toilets and windscreens. Manufactured without firing, the compressed lime bricks produce two-thirds less embodied carbon than conventional clay bricks and absorb carbon dioxide from the air as they cure.

fivew: Carmody Groarke, Atama and Re-st designed the new extension.

To unite existing museum wings and create a sustainable, community-focused civic space.

timeline.text: Job vacancies fall as small firms cut back on recruitment

gist: UK job vacancies dropped by 21,000 to 691,000, reaching a five-year low.
Smaller businesses cut hiring because of increased labour expenses and elevated energy bills.
The unemployment rate fell to 4.7%, though youth joblessness remains a concern.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: UK job openings fell by 21,000 to 691,000 during the three months to September, marking the lowest figure in more than five years. The steepest decline occurred within construction. Over the three months to August, the overall unemployment rate fell to 4.7%, while real earnings grew by 0.8%.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Smaller firms are curbing recruitment because of climbing staffing overheads, including statutory wage increases and National Insurance changes, alongside higher energy bills. Although ministers cited employment resilience, youth unemployment reached 15.6%, leaving nearly one million young individuals outside work, education, or training.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Chancellor John Healey presents his first Budget next week, whilst analysts expect hiring to stay subdued due to persistent energy costs.

fivew: Job vacancies fell to their lowest level in over five years.

sections.text: Three Jewish women reported being attacked in north-east London. Members of a Jewish neighbourhood watch group detained a suspect before police arrived and made an arrest.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Police treated the event as a suspected antisemitic hate crime, prompting heightened patrols and discussions with local community leaders to offer reassurance.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The suspect remains in custody following further arrest for a separate incident, while police appeal for witnesses and additional victims.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Arsenal struggled to break down a deep Forest defence before finding a late breakthrough. With ten minutes remaining, Declan Rice set up Madueke, whose effort deflected off Jair Cunha into the net. Forest threatened when Murillo almost produced an injury-time equaliser, whilst Daniel Munoz tested goalkeeper David Raya. Arsenal preserved a clean sheet, supported by a decisive stoppage-time tackle by Ezri Konsa on Liam Delap.

sections.text: Wiegman has led the Lionesses to two consecutive European Championship titles and reached five major finals in a row. The deal prevents speculation about her future, giving the team stability. FA chief Mark Bullingham commended her tournament achievements and leadership.

gist: Sonay Kartal lost the Wuhan Open final to Poland's Maja Chwalinska.

Kartal will rise to 50th in the world rankings and British number one.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Britain's Sonay Kartal lost 2-6 6-4 6-2 to Poland's Maja Chwalinska in the Wuhan Open final in China. Playing in just her tenth match since returning from a six-month back injury, 24-year-old Kartal won the first set and led in the second before Chwalinska fought back to win her first WTA 1,000 title.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Kartal reached her biggest career final after defeating high-profile opponents, including former major champions and top-10 players, despite entering the tournament using a protected injury ranking.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Kartal will climb to 50th in the world rankings on Monday, achieving a new position as the British number one for the first time.

sections.text: Racing Bulls is deciding its 2027 driver line-up between Liam Lawson, Arvid Lindblad, and Nikola Tsolov. Meanwhile, F1 announced a future grand prix in Rwanda, while keeping Imola on standby as a back-up track for the final race of the season because of potential instability in the Middle East.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The Racing Bulls decision marks the first time Helmut Marko is not choosing junior drivers. sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Shareholders and executives will decide the Racing Bulls driver line-up. F1 continues to monitor security in the Middle East ahead of the final races, with an agreement in place to cover Imola's costs if it needs to step in as a venue.

gist: REDs is a serious health condition caused by low energy availability in sport.
Male athletes often suffer from REDs in silence due to stigma and lack of awareness.
Sports organisations are increasingly introducing education, health screenings, and preventative measures.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Athletes like Jake Smith and Brian Smith suffered severe injuries and health issues due to under-fuelling and REDs, driven by the sports culture of being as light as possible.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: REDs causes hormonal disruption, bone stress injuries, and long-term health problems. While women have menstrual cycles as a warning sign, men suffer more subtle symptoms and face stigma.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Experts and organisations are pushing for better education, nutrition advice, and mandatory health screenings to help athletes prevent and recover from REDs.

fivew: Male and female athletes in endurance and weight-sensitive sports.
Athletes are suffering from relative energy deficiency in sport, known as REDs.
Recently, as highlighted by a meta-analysis and ongoing athlete accounts.
Globally in sports, including elite and amateur levels.
Because of insufficient energy intake driven by the belief that lighter is faster and a lack of awareness.

quotes.text: If you keep this up, you'll be in a wheelchair at 30.
